conventions.convention: Learned models share nonempty finite state/action domains with the true model; true rewards and estimated reward means lie in [0,1]. Transition error is total variation, equal to half the finite L1 distance. Both uniform errors on an empty pair set are defined as zero.
Finite-horizon return uses H≥1, time indices 0 through H−1, a possibly randomized time-dependent Markov policy, no discount, and no terminal continuation value.

SSP goals have exactly one absorbing action with deterministic zero reward. Every nonglobal expected cost is at least a common c_min>0. Proper stationary policies have survival probabilities tending to zero from every initial state; their existence is a separate hypothesis.

RTDP computes action values from the pre-backup table, executes a fresh uniform greedy action, and updates only the current state. Trial resets change no table entry and are not Bellman transitions. Reward values V correspond to costs f through V=−f.

RTDP recurrent-state convergence requires outcome-backup fairness. Convergence at all optimal-relevant states additionally requires Bellman-subsolution initialization f_0≤Tf_0; non-overestimating initialization alone does not provide it.

Dyna-Q is restricted to deterministic rewards and transitions, queries only previously experienced pairs, and samples a seen state uniformly followed by a seen action uniformly. It makes no convergence claim.
MPC receives a complete ordered action listing at every state, uses it for deterministic tie-breaking, and executes only the first action of its horizon-H plan.

Off-support exploitation is relative to an observed-pair set B and a finite nonempty deterministic Markov-policy class. It requires learned-model optimality, positive learned occupancy outside B, strict overprediction, and strict true suboptimality within that class.

load_bearing.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and a finite positive-cost SSP with at least one proper stationary policy. The infimum of total expected cost over all history-dependent policies is finite at every state, is the unique finite nonnegative solution of the stated goal-zero Bellman equations, and is attained from every initial state by a proper deterministic stationary minimizing policy.

On the true finite MDP's common nonempty finite state/action domain, a learned model supplies reward estimates in [0,1] and a probability transition row at every admissible pair. Reward error is the absolute difference of reward means; transition error is half the L1 difference of transition rows. Uniform errors on a nonempty pair set are their maxima, and on the empty set both are zero.

For finite nonempty state/action sets, probability transition rows P and P-hat, policy rows π, and state laws d and d-hat, if row TV error is at most ε≥0 whenever d-hat(s)>0 and π(a|s)>0, then TV(dK^π,d-hat K-hat^π)≤TV(d,d-hat)+ε.

For two finite models on common nonempty finite state/action sets with reward means in [0,1], a common initial law, H≥1, and one fixed possibly time-dependent randomized Markov policy, reward and transition-TV errors bounded by ε_r and ε_p on the union of true and learned reachable pairs imply |J_H−J-hat_H|≤Hε_r+binom(H,2)ε_p. This does not bound a policy selected by optimizing the learned model.

A finite SSP has a nonempty finite state set, finite nonempty action sets, a nonempty goal set with singleton absorbing zero-reward actions, and a common strictly positive lower bound on nonglobal expected costs. A stationary policy is proper precisely when its recursively defined finite-step survival probabilities tend to zero from every state. A proper policy need not exist.

For H≥1, finite probability transition rows, reward means in [0,1], initial law μ, and time-dependent Markov policy rows π_t, propagate the state laws from d_0=μ and sum d_t(s)π_t(a|s)r(s,a) over t=0,…,H−1 and all admissible pairs. The learned-model return replaces r and P by their estimates.

published_dependencies.used_for: Explicit choice hypothesis in SSP existence, asynchronous iteration, and RTDP convergence; inherited path-law and conditional-expectation assumptions.
Pointwise probability-row and measurable-section requirements for finite transition tables and policy mixtures.
Finite half-L1 formula and equal positive/negative mass of a difference of probability laws.
Applying one probability kernel to two laws cannot increase their total variation.
Attainment of finite action extrema, finite error maxima, and finite policy-class return maxima.
Nonnegativity, sign symmetry, and multiplicativity of absolute value.
Two-term scalar triangle inequalities in model-error and return estimates.
Finite-sum triangle inequalities in policy mixtures and accumulated return error.
Expansion, scaling, and monotonicity of finite sums in the TV propagation proof.
Enumeration-independent finite sums and bijective reindexing in TV propagation.
Existence of history-dependent policy trajectory laws under the stated AC hypothesis.
Limits of bounded monotone real sequences, rather than interchange of limits and integrals.
Iterating bounded finite-prefix conditional expectations and conditional avoidance estimates in RTDP.

concerns.concern: Proof 2.1 says 'The scalar triangle inequality [F5]'. F5 cites lem-of-abs-value and states nonnegativity and multiplicativity, not the triangle inequality. The argument is valid using the already supplied finite-sum triangle inequality F6 with two terms, but the specific F5 attribution is inaccurate.

seams_checked.note: Read the prerequisite page and def-finite-markov-decision-process. The learned-model branch explicitly restricts rewards to [0,1] and states to nonempty sets; the SSP branch separately uses negative expected rewards and absorbing singleton goal actions. Both correctly derive P and r from the joint reward-transition law. No discounted Bellman theorem is used as an undiscounted SSP supplier.

Read the prerequisite page, alg-q-learning, and def-optimal-action-value-bellman-operator. Dyna-Q uses the same single-coordinate reward-plus-discounted-greedy-continuation update, specializes the environment to deterministic responses, and makes no claim to inherit stochastic-approximation convergence. The cited procedure and its actual use agree.
